title: Hugging Face
blurb: The toolkit real AI engineers use daily: the Hub, transformers, datasets, pipeline(), fine-tuning, and publishing your own models.

lessons.title: The Hugging Face Hub & ecosystem overview
objectives: Explain what the Hugging Face Hub hosts and how the ecosystem's pieces fit together
Explain how Hugging Face Hub changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Hugging Face Hub with transformers library and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The Hugging Face Hub is a public repository of pretrained models, datasets, and demo apps (Spaces) -- hundreds of thousands of models covering text, vision, and audio, each identified by a namespace like 'bert-base-uncased' or 'meta-llama/Llama-2-7b'.
examples:
# the ecosystem's pieces:
# Hub          -- where models/datasets/demos are hosted
# transformers -- library to load and run models from the Hub
# datasets     -- library to load and process datasets from the Hub
# both transformers and datasets run ON TOP of PyTorch or TensorFlow,
# the frameworks you already know from those tracks
commonMistakes: Assuming Hugging Face is a separate deep learning framework competing with PyTorch/TensorFlow -- it's a layer built on top of them, providing pretrained models and easy loading/training.
lessons.careerRelevance: Hugging Face is the de facto standard toolkit real AI engineering teams use daily to work with pretrained models, not just a nice-to-have.

lessons.title: pipeline(): the fastest path to a working model
objectives: Use pipeline() to run a pretrained model in a few lines of code
Explain how pipeline() changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect pipeline() with task-based API and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: pipeline() is the highest-level API in `transformers` -- given a task name (like 'sentiment-analysis' or 'text-generation'), it automatically downloads a sensible pretrained model, its tokenizer, and wraps pre/post-processing into one callable object.
examples:
from transformers import pipeline
classifier = pipeline('sentiment-analysis')
result = classifier('This course is great!')
# [{'label': 'POSITIVE', 'score': 0.9998}]
commonMistakes: Using pipeline() for every production use case without checking which default model it picked -- for anything beyond quick prototyping, explicitly specify the model so you know exactly.
lessons.careerRelevance: pipeline() is genuinely how most real prototyping with pretrained models starts, even at companies with mature ML infrastructure.
lessons.explain: pipeline() is the highest-level API in `transformers` -- given a task name (like 'sentiment-analysis' or 'text-generation'), it automatically downloads a sensible pretrained model, its tokenizer, and wraps pre/post-processing into one callable object.
lessons.example:
from transformers import pipeline
classifier = pipeline('sentiment-analysis')

# [{'label': 'POSITIVE', 'score': 0.9998}]

lessons.title: Loading pretrained models & tokenizers directly
objectives: Load a specific model and tokenizer using the Auto classes
Explain how AutoModel changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect AutoModel with AutoTokenizer and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: AutoModel and AutoTokenizer let you load any model from the Hub by name, automatically picking the right architecture class based on the model's config -- you don't need to know in advance whether it's BERT, RoBERTa, or something else.
examples:
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('bert-base-uncased')
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained('bert-base-uncased')

inputs = tokenizer('Hello world', return_tensors='pt')
outputs = model(**inputs)
commonMistakes: Loading a model with one name but its tokenizer with a different, similar-sounding model name -- token IDs are meaningless outside the exact vocabulary they were trained with, so this.
lessons.careerRelevance: AutoModel/AutoTokenizer are the standard, correct way to load any Hub model when you need more control than pipeline() gives you.
lessons.explain: AutoModel and AutoTokenizer let you load any model from the Hub by name, automatically picking the right architecture class based on the model's config -- you don't need to know in advance whether it's BERT, RoBERTa, or something else.
lessons.example:
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('bert-base-uncased')
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained('bert-base-uncased')

inputs = tokenizer('Hello world', return_tensors='pt')
outputs = model(**inputs)

lessons.title: Tokenizers in practice
objectives: Use a Hugging Face tokenizer's practical output correctly
Explain how input_ids changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect input_ids with attention_mask and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: You already know conceptually why sub-word tokenization exists (from the Transformers and LLMs tracks) -- this lesson is about using the actual tokenizer object. Calling a tokenizer returns input_ids (the token IDs the model expects) and an attention_mask (marking real tokens vs padding, so the model ignores padded positions).
examples:
tokenizer(['Hi', 'A much longer sentence here'], padding=True, truncation=True, return_tensors='pt')
# input_ids:      padded token ID sequences, same length across the batch
# attention_mask:  1s for real tokens, 0s for padding -- tells the model what to ignore
commonMistakes: Forgetting padding=True when tokenizing a batch of different-length sequences -- this causes a shape-mismatch error, since the model needs every sequence in a batch to be the same length.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correctly handling padding/attention masks is a real, common source of subtle bugs in practical Hugging Face code.
lessons.explain: You already know conceptually why sub-word tokenization exists (from the Transformers and LLMs tracks) -- this lesson is about using the actual tokenizer object. lessons.title: Text classification & common pipeline tasks
objectives: Apply pretrained models to common text tasks beyond sentiment analysis
Explain how zero-shot classification changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect zero-shot classification with named entity recognition and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Beyond sentiment analysis, common ready-to-use tasks include zero-shot-classification (classify text into labels the model was never explicitly trained on, by comparing against candidate label descriptions), named-entity-recognition (tagging people/places/organizations in text), and summarization.
examples:
classifier = pipeline('zero-shot-classification')
classifier('This is a course about Kubernetes', candidate_labels=['education', 'sports', 'cooking'])
# scores each candidate label WITHOUT the model ever being trained on these exact labels

lessons.careerRelevance: Zero-shot classification specifically is a genuinely practical technique for handling new label categories without collecting training data first.

lessons.title: Embeddings & feature extraction
objectives: Generate and use embeddings from a Hugging Face model
Explain how feature extraction changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect feature extraction with sentence embeddings and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The 'feature-extraction' pipeline task (or calling a model directly and taking its output hidden states) turns text into a dense vector embedding -- the same underlying concept covered in the RAG track's embeddings lesson, but here using the actual Hugging Face tooling to produce them.
examples:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
model = SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2')
embeddings = model.encode(['a sentence', 'another sentence'])
# ready to feed into the vector DB / similarity search covered in the RAG track
commonMistakes: Using a plain `transformers` model's raw hidden states directly for sentence similarity without pooling -- sentence-transformers models are specifically tuned to produce good whole-sentence.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is the exact practical bridge between the RAG track's embedding theory and a real, runnable embeddings pipeline you'd deploy.

lessons.title: The datasets library
objectives: Load, inspect, and preprocess a dataset from the Hub
Explain how datasets library changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect datasets library with load_dataset and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The `datasets` library loads datasets from the Hub (or your own files) into a memory-efficient format, with a consistent API across wildly different dataset sizes -- from a few hundred rows to datasets larger than your machine's RAM, using memory-mapping so you don't need to load everything at once.
examples:
from datasets import load_dataset
dataset = load_dataset('imdb')
tokenized = dataset.map(lambda x: tokenizer(x['text'], truncation=True), batched=True)
commonMistakes: Manually writing a custom data-loading pipeline for a public dataset that's already on the Hub -- load_dataset handles this consistently and efficiently, and reinventing it wastes real time.
lessons.careerRelevance: Fluency with the datasets library is assumed alongside `transformers` in any real Hugging Face fine-tuning workflow.
lessons.explain: The `datasets` library loads datasets from the Hub (or your own files) into a memory-efficient format, with a consistent API across wildly different dataset sizes -- from a few hundred rows to datasets larger than your machine's RAM, using memory-mapping so you don't need to load everything at once.

lessons.title: Authentication, access tokens & gated models
objectives: Authenticate with the Hub and access gated models correctly
Explain how access token changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect access token with gated model and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Some models on the Hub are gated -- you must accept a license agreement on the model's page before you're allowed to download it (common for newer, more powerful models like Llama). Authenticating with an access token (via `huggingface-cli login` or passing a token directly) is required both for gated models and for uploading your own models/datasets.
examples:
from huggingface_hub import login
login(token='hf_...')  # or set the HF_TOKEN environment variable

# gated models require BOTH a valid token AND having accepted
# that specific model's license on the Hub website first
commonMistakes: Hardcoding an access token directly in a script that gets committed to a public GitHub repo -- treat Hugging Face tokens exactly like any other secret credential, using environment.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correctly handling gated-model access and tokens is a routine practical requirement once you work with newer, license-restricted models.

lessons.title: Fine-tuning with Trainer
objectives: Fine-tune a pretrained model using the Trainer API
Explain how Trainer changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Trainer with TrainingArguments and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The Trainer class wraps the training loop concepts you already know from PyTorch (forward pass, loss, backward, optimizer step) into a configurable, batteries-included API -- handling the loop, evaluation, checkpointing, and logging for you, driven by a TrainingArguments object specifying epochs, batch size, learning rate, and more.
examples:
from transformers import Trainer, TrainingArguments

args = TrainingArguments(output_dir='./results', num_train_epochs=3, per_device_train_batch_size=16)
trainer = Trainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=tokenized['train'], eval_dataset=tokenized['test'])
trainer.train()
commonMistakes: Fine-tuning on far too few epochs/examples and expecting strong results -- fine-tuning still needs a reasonable amount of representative labeled data; it adapts a pretrained model, it.
lessons.careerRelevance: Trainer-based fine-tuning is the standard, expected workflow for adapting a pretrained model to a specific task or domain in real projects.
lessons.explain: The Trainer class wraps the training loop concepts you already know from PyTorch (forward pass, loss, backward, optimizer step) into a configurable, batteries-included API -- handling the loop, evaluation, checkpointing, and logging for you, driven by a TrainingArguments object specifying epochs, batch size, learning rate, and more.
lessons.example:
from transformers import Trainer, TrainingArguments

args = TrainingArguments(output_dir='./results', num_train_epochs=3, per_device_train_batch_size=16)
trainer = Trainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=tokenized['train'], eval_dataset=tokenized['test'])
trainer.train()

lessons.title: Saving, publishing, Spaces & Gradio

lessons.explanation: model.save_pretrained() and tokenizer.save_pretrained() save everything needed to reload a model later; push_to_hub() uploads it directly to your own Hub namespace, alongside your model card.
commonMistakes: Publishing a model without saving the tokenizer alongside it -- a model with no matching tokenizer is effectively unusable by anyone who downloads it later.

lessons.title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning: LoRA and QLoRA
objectives: Explain LoRA and QLoRA conceptually, and choose between full fine-tuning, LoRA, and QLoRA for a given constraint
Explain how LoRA (rank, alpha, target modules, dropout) changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect LoRA (rank, alpha, target modules, dropout) with QLoRA (quantized-base training) and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Full fine-tuning updates every parameter in a model -- expensive in memory and compute, and requires storing a full new copy of the model per fine-tuned variant.
examples:
# the core trade-off, without matrix derivations:
# full fine-tuning: EVERY parameter trains -- most capacity, most memory/compute cost
# LoRA: base model FROZEN, small adapter matrices train -- far less memory, a
# small extra file saved separately from the (unchanged) base model
# QLoRA: LoRA's adapter training, but the FROZEN base model is also quantized
# during training specifically to fit in less memory -- this is TRAINING-time
# quantization of the base, not the same as quantizing a model for inference only
commonMistakes: Assuming QLoRA and inference-time quantization are the same technique -- QLoRA quantizes the frozen base model specifically to make TRAINING fit in less memory, while inference quantization.
lessons.careerRelevance: LoRA and QLoRA are now the standard, default way most real fine-tuning work is actually done in practice, given how much cheaper they are than full fine-tuning for most use cases.
lessons.explain: Full fine-tuning updates every parameter in a model -- expensive in memory and compute, and requires storing a full new copy of the model per fine-tuned variant.

lessons.title: Preparing and Validating a Fine-Tuning Run
objectives: Prepare a well-formed instruction dataset, understand label masking, and evaluate whether an adaptation actually helped without damaging other capabilities
Explain how conversational dataset formatting changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect conversational dataset formatting with label masking and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A fine-tuning run needs a valid dataset, training configuration, and evaluation plan before you spend significant compute. This lesson shows how to prepare the inputs, validate the setup with a small check first, and use evaluation results to decide whether the full run is behaving correctly.
examples:
# why label masking matters -- training on the WRONG tokens changes the task:
# unmasked (wrong): the model is trained to predict BOTH the prompt AND the
# response -- it partly learns to predict user questions, which isn't the goal
# masked correctly: the model is trained to predict ONLY the assistant's
# response tokens, given the prompt as fixed context -- this is what instruction
# tuning is actually supposed to teach it to do
commonMistakes: Judging a fine-tuning run only by whether validation loss went down -- a lower loss doesn't guarantee the task-specific behavior actually improved, and doesn't check at all whether the model.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correctly masking labels and rigorously checking for catastrophic forgetting (not just validation loss) are exactly the practical details that separate a genuinely useful fine-tuning workflow from one that looks fine in a training log but fails in practice.

quiz.q: What does push_to_hub() do?
options: deletes a model from the Hub
uploads a model (and typically its tokenizer) directly to your Hub namespace
only downloads models, never uploads
trains a model remotely on Hugging Face's servers

quiz.q: What is a Hugging Face Space?
options: a private, unlisted model
a free-hosted demo app on the Hub, commonly built with Gradio
a synonym for a dataset
a paid-only feature

quiz.q: What does Gradio let you do?
options: only visualize training metrics
turn a Python function into a shareable web UI in a few lines of code
only work with image data
replace the need for a trained model entirely

quiz.q: What does load_in_8bit=True do when loading a model?
options: deletes half the model's layers
quantizes the model to lower precision, reducing memory use at a small accuracy cost
doubles the model's accuracy
only affects the tokenizer, not the model

quiz.q: In a real system, how does a Hugging Face model typically get used?
options: as the entire standalone application with no other components
as one component wrapped behind an API, feeding a RAG pipeline, or serving as a tool an agent calls
Hugging Face models can't be integrated with other systems
only inside a Jupyter notebook, never in production

quiz.q: What is the main practical difference between full fine-tuning and PEFT approaches like LoRA?
options: They are functionally identical
Full fine-tuning updates every model parameter; PEFT freezes the base model and trains a small number of additional adapter parameters instead
PEFT always produces better results than full fine-tuning
Full fine-tuning requires no GPU at all

quiz.q: What do LoRA's rank and alpha settings conceptually control?
options: Nothing meaningful
Rank controls the adapter's trainable capacity; alpha scales how strongly the adapter's update affects the frozen base model's output
Rank and alpha are the same setting under two names
These settings only affect inference speed, not training

quiz.q: How does QLoRA differ from inference-time quantization?
options: They are the same technique
QLoRA quantizes the frozen base model specifically to make training fit in less memory; inference quantization reduces precision purely to make serving cheaper or faster
QLoRA only applies to already-deployed models
Inference quantization requires LoRA adapters to function

quiz.q: Why is validation loss alone insufficient to confirm fine-tuning improved a model?
options: Validation loss is always a complete, sufficient signal
A lower loss doesn't guarantee task-specific behavior actually improved, and doesn't check whether the model lost other capability it previously had (catastrophic forgetting)
Validation loss should never be measured
Loss and catastrophic forgetting are the same measurement

exercises.title: Run your first pipeline
exercises.prompt: Write code using pipeline() to classify the sentiment of 'I love this course.'

exercises.title: Load a model and tokenizer directly
exercises.prompt: Load 'distilbert-base-uncased' with AutoModel and AutoTokenizer, then tokenize a sentence.

exercises.title: Diagnose a tokenizer mismatch bug
exercises.prompt: A model produces nonsense output. You discover the tokenizer being used is from a different model than the one loaded. Explain why this causes silent nonsense rather than a clear error.
exercises.hint: token IDs are only meaningful relative to the exact vocabulary they were trained with

exercises.title: Diagnose a batch padding error
exercises.prompt: Tokenizing a batch of different-length sentences throws a shape-mismatch error. What's missing from the tokenizer call, and why does it fix this?
exercises.hint: padding=True -- pads all sequences in the batch to the same length, which models require

exercises.title: Generate sentence embeddings
exercises.prompt: Write code using sentence-transformers to generate embeddings for 3 sentences, ready to feed into a vector database.

exercises.title: Load and preprocess a dataset
exercises.prompt: Write code to load the 'imdb' dataset and tokenize its text field using .map().

exercises.title: Choose quantization or not
exercises.prompt: You need to run a large model on a machine with limited memory, and can accept a small accuracy trade-off. What technique fits, and how would you apply it?

exercises.title: Design a fine-tuning plan
exercises.prompt: You have 2,000 labeled support tickets and want to fine-tune a classifier. Outline your plan: model choice, TrainingArguments settings to consider, and how you'd evaluate the result.

exercises.title: Choose Full Fine-Tuning vs. LoRA vs. QLoRA
exercises.prompt: Given a 7B model, 16GB of GPU memory, and a dataset of 3,000 examples, choose and justify an approach: full fine-tuning, LoRA, or QLoRA.
exercises.hint: QLoRA -- a 7B model with only 16GB of memory is unlikely to fit full fine-tuning or even standard LoRA training comfortably; quantizing the frozen base model during training makes this fit

exercises.title: Diagnose a Fine-Tuning Dataset
exercises.prompt: A training dataset contains an example with two consecutive user turns and no assistant response, another example duplicated verbatim, and one where the expected answer already appears in the prompt. Diagnose each issue.
exercises.hint: invalid role sequence (two consecutive user turns), missing assistant response (no final assistant turn), duplicate training example, and response leakage (answer already present in the prompt) -- each is a distinct, separately-diagnosable problem

exercises.title: Diagnose Catastrophic Forgetting
exercises.prompt: After fine-tuning, a model's target-task accuracy improved significantly, but it now fails at general capabilities it previously handled well. Is this useful specialization, overfitting, or catastrophic forgetting?
exercises.hint: catastrophic forgetting -- the model gained the new specialized skill but lost previously-working general capability, distinct from overfitting (which would show as poor generalization even on the target task itself)

capstone.title: Fine-tune, evaluate, and publish a real model with a working demo
capstone.description: Take a labeled text dataset (your own, or one from the Hub), fine-tune a pretrained model on it using Trainer, evaluate it honestly with real metrics, then publish the result: push the model and tokenizer to your own Hub namespace with a complete model card documenting its training data, metrics, and known limitations, and build a Gradio Space so anyone can try it in a browser with zero setup.
deliverables: A fine-tuned model trained with Trainer on a real, labeled dataset
Evaluation results using the evaluate library, not just a training-loss number
A complete, honest model card (training data, metrics, and at least one real known limitation)
A working Gradio Space demonstrating the model live
A short write-up explaining one integration point: how this model could feed a RAG pipeline, an agent's tool call, or an API endpoint
Justification of full fine-tuning vs. LoRA vs. QLoRA for this specific project
Documentation of at least one limitation or regression risk of the adapted model
capstone.portfolioTips: A live, working Space is one of the most concrete things you can link directly in a resume or GitHub profile -- unlike a screenshot or a notebook, a reviewer can actually try it themselves in seconds.

Uses Hugging Face tooling to fine-tune and deploy domain-specific NLP models for financial text analysis.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the difference between using pipeline() and loading a model with AutoModel directly?
interviewPreparation.a: pipeline() is the fastest path to a working model -- it picks a sensible default model and handles pre/post-processing automatically. AutoModel/AutoTokenizer give you direct, fine-grained control over exactly which model and tokenizer load and how you use them, which you need once you're past quick prototyping.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is it critical that a model and its tokenizer match exactly?
interviewPreparation.a: Token IDs are only meaningful relative to the exact vocabulary a model was trained with. Using a mismatched tokenizer doesn't throw an error -- it silently feeds the model IDs that mean something completely different than what it expects, producing nonsense output with no obvious signal something's wrong.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you approach fine-tuning a model on a small, domain-specific dataset?
interviewPreparation.a: Start with a pretrained model close to your domain if one exists, use Trainer with TrainingArguments tuned conservatively (fewer epochs, careful learning rate) since a small dataset overfits easily, and evaluate on a genuinely held-out set with the evaluate library rather than trusting training loss alone.

interviewPreparation.q: What would you check first if a fine-tuned model performs far worse than expected?
interviewPreparation.a: Whether the tokenizer matches the model, whether padding/truncation are handled consistently between training and inference, and whether the training data is genuinely representative of what the model will see in production -- these are the most common practical causes, not the model architecture itself.

interviewPreparation.q: How does quantization trade off against model quality, and when would you use it?
interviewPreparation.a: Quantization reduces numerical precision (e.g. to 8-bit) to shrink memory use and speed up inference, at a small, often acceptable accuracy cost. It's the right call when you need to fit a large model into limited memory or hit a latency target, and you've confirmed the accuracy trade-off is genuinely acceptable for your use case.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you integrate a Hugging Face model into a larger production system?
interviewPreparation.a: Almost never as a standalone application -- typically wrapped behind an API endpoint that other services call, feeding a RAG pipeline's retrieval or generation step, or serving as a tool an agent invokes. The model is one component; the surrounding system (auth, monitoring, integration) is what makes it actually usable in production.

interviewPreparation.q: When would you choose LoRA or QLoRA instead of full fine-tuning?
interviewPreparation.a: When GPU memory or cost constraints make full fine-tuning impractical, when the dataset is small enough that full fine-tuning risks overfitting, or when you want a small, portable, swappable adapter rather than a full new copy of the model -- QLoRA specifically when the base model itself needs to be quantized during training to fit available memory.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you determine whether fine-tuning improved the target task without damaging other important capabilities?
interviewPreparation.a: Compare the adapted model against the original baseline on both the target task and a set of general/unrelated capability checks, not just validation loss in isolation -- a genuine improvement should show gains on the target task while general capability checks remain stable, rather than task-specific improvement paired with a regression elsewhere (catastrophic forgetting).
